summary: A stocky, big-headed bird that looks dull brown when perched on a roadside wire, then opens its wings in flight to show electric bands of turquoise and deep violet-blue. In the breeding season the male tumbles and rolls through the air in display, the habit that gives rollers their name.
nativeRange: Iraq and the Persian Gulf east through Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka to Myanmar
abilities: Hunts by watching from an exposed perch, then dropping onto large insects, lizards and small frogs on the ground
Performs a rolling, diving aerial courtship display with loud harsh calls
Follows tractors, grass fires and grazing cattle to snatch flushed insects

animal.diet: Large insects (grasshoppers, crickets, beetles), also scorpions, small lizards, frogs and rodents
animal.habitat: Open cultivation, grassland, light woodland and roadsides with plenty of perches
animal.behaviour: Sits motionless on wires and dead branches for long spells, then drops to the ground for prey and returns to the same perch; in courtship it climbs steeply and plunges in twisting, rolling dives.
fieldMarks: Thickset bird with large head and strong dark bill
Perched: rufous-brown breast and back, lilac-streaked throat, blue crown
In flight: brilliant bands of pale turquoise and dark violet-blue across the wings
Square blue tail with a dark terminal band
animal.voice: Harsh, crow-like 'chack' and grating 'kak-kak' calls, loudest during the rolling display flight
animal.lookalikes: European roller (a passage migrant in Pakistan and NW India) has a plain pale-blue head and underparts with no brown or lilac breast; Indochinese roller (east of the Brahmaputra) has a dark purplish-brown face and breast without fine streaks.
animal.whereToSee: Common along roadsides and farmland across the Indus plains of Punjab and Sindh and over most of India; easy at Keoladeo (Bharatpur) and Ranthambore

lore: Its Hindi name Neelkanth ('blue throat') is an epithet of Shiva, and in much of north India seeing the bird on Dussehra is considered auspicious. It is the state bird of several Indian states, including Karnataka and Telangana.
funFact: The dull brown bird on the wire is the same one that flashes vivid blue in flight; the brightest colours are hidden on the wings until it moves.

summary: A swaggering brown starling with a black hood and a bare yellow patch of skin behind each eye, at home on every South Asian lawn, market and railway platform. Taken around the world to eat crop pests, it has become one of the most widespread and controversial birds on Earth.
nativeRange: Iran and Central Asia through Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka to Myanmar; introduced to Australia, South Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, Hawaii, Florida and many islands
abilities: Thrives in cities, nesting in wall cavities, street lights and buildings
Imitates other birds and, in captivity, human speech
Gathers in communal roosts of hundreds to thousands of birds at dusk
Aggressively evicts other hole-nesting birds from nest sites

animal.diet: Omnivore: insects (especially grasshoppers), fruit, grain, food scraps
animal.habitat: Towns, villages, farmland and open country near people
animal.behaviour: Walks rather than hops, striding across lawns; pairs bob their heads and fluff their plumage at each other in noisy displays, and flocks converge on huge evening roosts with deafening chatter.
fieldMarks: Warm brown body with glossy black head and breast
Bare yellow skin around and behind the eye; yellow bill and legs
Large white wing patch obvious in flight
White under-tail and white tail tip
animal.voice: Very varied: gurgles, chattering 'kok-kok-kok', squawks and liquid whistles; alarm a harsh 'chake-chake'
animal.lookalikes: Bank myna is greyer with a brick-red (not yellow) bare face patch; Jungle myna is slate-grey with a tuft of feathers at the bill base and no bare face patch; Asian pied starling is black-and-white.
animal.whereToSee: Every town and village in Pakistan, India and Sri Lanka, e.g. Lahore, Karachi, Delhi and Colombo parks

lore: Long kept as a talking cage-bird across the subcontinent. Introduced to Mauritius in the 1760s to control locusts and later to Australia and Hawaii, it is now listed among the IUCN Invasive Species Specialist Group's '100 of the World's Worst Invasive Alien Species'.
funFact: It is one of only three birds on the IUCN '100 worst invasive species' list; the Red-vented bulbul and the Common starling are the other two.

summary: The grey-necked crow of South Asian cities, living almost entirely alongside people and scavenging from markets, rubbish heaps and rooftops. Bold, intelligent and ship-borne, it has spread to ports from East Africa to the Netherlands.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, the Maldives and Myanmar; introduced to East Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, Singapore and elsewhere
abilities: Exploits human settlements so completely that it is rarely found away from people
Spreads by stowing away on ships, founding colonies in distant ports
Mobs predators in noisy groups and is host to the parasitic Asian koel
Gathers in communal roosts numbering thousands

animal.diet: Omnivorous scavenger: food waste, carrion, insects, eggs and nestlings, fruit and grain
animal.habitat: Cities, towns, villages and harbours
animal.behaviour: Highly social and quick to learn; groups gather around a dead crow and call loudly, and they steal food from people and other birds with practised timing.
fieldMarks: Medium-sized crow with glossy black face, crown, throat, wings and tail
Contrasting grey nape, neck and breast forming a collar
Relatively slim black bill and domed forehead
animal.voice: A flat, dry 'kaaw-kaaw', higher-pitched than the Large-billed crow
animal.lookalikes: Large-billed (Jungle) crow is all glossy black with a much heavier arched bill and deeper call.
animal.whereToSee: Every city of the subcontinent, from Karachi and Mumbai harbours to Colombo

lore: In Hindu ritual crows are fed rice balls (pinda) during shraddha and Pitru Paksha as messengers of the ancestors, and a crow cawing on the roof was said in Urdu and Hindi folklore to announce an arriving guest.
funFact: House crows reached Hoek van Holland in the Netherlands by ship and bred there, thousands of kilometres from the nearest native population.

summary: A large cuckoo whose rising, insistent 'ko-EL, ko-EL' is the sound of the South Asian hot season, often heard long before dawn. It lays its eggs in the nests of crows, which raise the koel chicks as their own.
nativeRange: Pakistan and India through Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and southern China to Southeast Asia and the Greater Sundas
abilities: Brood parasite: lays eggs in House crow and Large-billed crow nests in South Asia
Male lures crows away from the nest while the female slips in to lay
Unusually for cuckoos, adults are largely fruit-eaters, dispersing seeds of figs and other trees

animal.diet: Mainly fruit and berries (figs, peepal, banyan); also insects and caterpillars
animal.habitat: Leafy gardens, orchards, groves and open woodland
animal.behaviour: Skulks in dense foliage and is heard far more than seen; the male calls repeatedly from cover, each phrase rising in pitch and urgency.
fieldMarks: Male entirely glossy blue-black with a pale greenish bill and crimson eye
Female brown, heavily spotted and barred with white and buff
Long tail and slim, rather crow-like build
Red eye in both sexes
animal.voice: Male: a loud, rising 'ko-el, ko-EL, KO-EL', repeated in crescendo; also a bubbling 'kuil-kuil-kuil'. Female: a shrill 'kik-kik-kik'.
animal.lookalikes: The black male could be mistaken for a crow or drongo, but has a red eye, pale bill and long rounded tail; Greater coucal is larger with rufous wings.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens and avenues across Pakistan and India, from Lahore's Jinnah Garden to Delhi's Lodhi Garden
animal.season: Resident in much of its range; most vocal March–August; in northern Pakistan a summer visitor

lore: As the kokila it is a symbol of spring and longing in Sanskrit poetry, including Kalidasa, and the koyal remains a byword for a sweet voice in Urdu, Hindi and Punjabi songs.
funFact: A koel's voice is sweet only to people: crows recognise the bird as a threat and chase it furiously.

otherNames: Hēi hóu hóng tún bēi 黑喉红臀鹎 (Chinese)
summary: A perky, crested garden bird with a black head and a scarlet patch under the tail, one of the most familiar voices in South Asian courtyards. Cheerful to people but invasive on Pacific islands, it is an expert disperser of berry seeds.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar to SW China; introduced to Hawaii, Fiji, Samoa, Tonga and parts of the Arabian Peninsula
abilities: Disperses seeds of shrubs such as lantana, which has helped its spread on islands
Lives comfortably in gardens and will nest on verandas and in hanging plants
Pairs mob snakes, cats and owls with loud alarm calls

animal.diet: Fruit, berries, nectar, petals and insects
animal.habitat: Gardens, scrub, farmland edges and dry open woodland
animal.behaviour: Pairs keep up a constant cheerful chatter, and the male displays by fluffing his white rump and spreading his tail to show the red vent.
fieldMarks: Short black crest and black head, throat and breast
Scaly dark-brown back and breast
Bright crimson undertail (vent) and white rump
Dark tail with white tip
animal.voice: Cheery, rather fluty 'be-care-ful' or 'ginger beer' phrases and a sharp 'peep-peep' alarm
animal.lookalikes: Red-whiskered bulbul has a tall pointed crest, white cheeks and a red whisker patch; Himalayan bulbul (northern Pakistan) has a white cheek and yellow vent; White-eared bulbul (Sindh/Punjab) has white cheeks and a yellow vent.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens and parks throughout Pakistan and India, e.g. Islamabad's Margalla foothills, Lahore and Karachi gardens

lore: The 'bulbul' of Persian and Urdu poetry is really the nightingale, but in South Asia the name passed to these garden birds. In Assam, captive bulbuls were traditionally set to fight at Hajo's Hayagriva Madhava temple during Magh Bihu.
funFact: It is on the IUCN list of the 100 worst invasive alien species because of its effects on Pacific island crops and native birds.

summary: A tiny nectar-feeder whose breeding male is glossy purple-black that flashes metallic blue and green in the sun. It fills the ecological role hummingbirds play in the Americas, but usually perches rather than hovers to feed.
nativeRange: The Persian Gulf, Oman and Iran through Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka to Myanmar and Indochina
abilities: Pollinates many flowering plants as it feeds on nectar with a long, curved bill and tubular tongue
Can hover briefly at flowers like a hummingbird
Weaves a hanging purse-shaped nest bound with spider silk and decorated with debris
Pierces the base of long tubular flowers to 'rob' nectar

animal.diet: Nectar, small insects and spiders
animal.habitat: Gardens, dry scrub, thorn forest and open woodland
animal.behaviour: Restless and quick, flicking its wings as it moves between flowers; the hanging nest often has a little porch over the side entrance.
fieldMarks: Very small with a long, down-curved black bill
Breeding male: all glossy purple-black, iridescent in sunlight, with yellow and orange tufts under the wing in display
Female: olive-brown above, pale yellow below
Non-breeding male resembles female but with a dark stripe down the centre of the breast
animal.voice: Sharp, metallic 'chwit' or 'zit' calls; male sings a rapid, twittering 'cheewit-cheewit-swee'
animal.lookalikes: Purple-rumped sunbird (peninsular India, Sri Lanka) has a maroon back and yellow belly; Loten's sunbird has a much longer bill and a maroon breast band.
animal.whereToSee: Flowering gardens across Pakistan and India; common on bottlebrush and hibiscus in Karachi, Lahore and Delhi
animal.season: Resident; males in breeding plumage mainly in spring and summer

lore: Its Urdu and Hindi name shakar khora means 'sugar eater'.
funFact: In the Old World, sunbirds evolved to fill the nectar-feeding niche independently of the New World hummingbirds, a classic case of convergent evolution.

otherNames: Hóng lǐng lǜ yīngwǔ 红领绿鹦鹉 (Chinese)
summary: A bright green, long-tailed parrot whose screeching flocks streak over South Asian cities and farmland. It is among the most successful parrots on Earth, with feral colonies thriving in London, Amsterdam, Istanbul and dozens of other cities.
nativeRange: Sahel belt of Africa and the Indian subcontinent (Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka) to Myanmar; feral populations across Europe, the Middle East, East Asia and the Americas
abilities: Survives freezing European winters in feral colonies by exploiting garden bird feeders
Learns human speech well in captivity
Raids orchards and grain fields in large flocks, cracking seeds with its hooked bill
Nests early in tree holes, competing with native hole-nesters

animal.diet: Seeds, grain, fruit, buds, flowers and nectar
animal.habitat: Open woodland, farmland, orchards, parks and city avenues
animal.size: About 40 cm including the long tail
animal.behaviour: Gathers in large, raucous communal roosts in city trees each evening; pairs nest in natural holes or excavate soft wood.
fieldMarks: Bright green with a very long, pointed blue-green tail
Deep red hooked bill
Male has a black chin stripe and a thin rose-pink and black neck ring; females and young lack the ring
Fast, direct flight with rapid wingbeats
animal.voice: Loud, shrill screeching 'kee-ak' calls, especially in flight
animal.lookalikes: Alexandrine parakeet is much larger with a heavier bill and a maroon shoulder patch; Plum-headed parakeet has a plum-red (male) or grey (female) head; Slaty-headed parakeet (Himalaya) has a grey head.
animal.whereToSee: Abundant in cities and farmland across Pakistan and India, from Lahore and Islamabad to Delhi; also London's parks

lore: In Indian myth the parrot (shuka) is the mount of Kamadeva, god of love, and the sage Shuka narrates the Bhagavata Purana. On South Asian streets, trained parakeets still pick fortune cards for passers-by.
funFact: Feral rose-ringed parakeets have bred in Britain since at least the late 1960s, and the London population numbers in the tens of thousands.

summary: A medium-sized brown raptor with a forked tail that wheels in hundreds over South Asian cities, scavenging from rubbish dumps, slaughterhouses and markets. It is likely one of the most numerous birds of prey in the world.
nativeRange: Much of Europe, Africa, Asia and Australia; absent from the Americas
abilities: Steers with its long forked tail, twisting it constantly to manoeuvre in crowded city air
Snatches food from the ground, water or even people's hands in flight without landing
Northern populations migrate thousands of kilometres, while South Asian city birds are resident
Gathers at grass fires to catch fleeing insects and small animals

animal.diet: Carrion, refuse, fish, rodents, insects, small birds; opportunistic scavenger
animal.habitat: Cities, villages, river banks, wetlands and open country
animal.size: About 50–60 cm long; wingspan about 130–155 cm
animal.behaviour: Soars and circles over cities for hours, then swoops down to snatch scraps with its feet; on summer days flocks of hundreds may circle together.
fieldMarks: Dark brown raptor with a long, shallowly forked tail (looks square when fully spread)
Long angled wings with a pale panel on the upperwing and paler 'windows' near the wingtips below
Pale head with dark eye-patch; yellow feet
Constant twisting of the tail in flight
animal.voice: A high, quavering whinny 'pee-errrr', often given in flight
animal.lookalikes: Brahminy kite is chestnut with a white head and a rounded tail; Red kite (rare in Asia) is rufous with a deeply forked tail; Marsh harriers have long unforked tails and glide with raised wings.
animal.whereToSee: Over every large South Asian city, especially Delhi, Lahore, Karachi and Dhaka
animal.season: Resident in South Asian cities; the black-eared form is a winter visitor from Central and East Asia

lore: In Delhi's Wazirabad, brothers Nadeem Shehzad and Mohammad Saud have rescued thousands of injured kites, many cut by kite-flying strings; their work is the subject of the 2022 documentary 'All That Breathes'.
funFact: Black kites in northern Australia have been documented picking up burning sticks and dropping them to spread grass fires, flushing prey.

summary: A small, pale grey hawk that hunts lizards and birds in gardens and groves across South Asia and Africa. Its name comes from the same root as 'shikar', the hunt, and it was flown by falconers in the subcontinent.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa and from southern Central Asia and Iran through Pakistan, India and Sri Lanka to southern China and Southeast Asia
abilities: Ambushes prey from a hidden perch with a short, fast dash
Takes many lizards and large insects from the ground, as well as small birds
Lives quietly in city parks and gardens, often unnoticed

animal.diet: Lizards, small birds, rodents, large insects and frogs
animal.habitat: Open woodland, groves, gardens and farmland
animal.behaviour: Sits in a leafy tree and launches a short, rapid attack, flying low and fast; small birds give sharp alarm calls when it appears, and Black drongos imitate its call.
fieldMarks: Small hawk with short rounded wings and a medium tail
Adult pale blue-grey above with fine rufous barring below
Thin dark stripe down the centre of the throat
Red (male) or yellow (female) eye; yellow legs
animal.voice: A loud, shrill 'ti-tui' or 'kik-ki', repeated; often heard before it is seen
animal.lookalikes: Eurasian sparrowhawk (winter in Pakistan and the Himalaya) has a longer tail and darker grey back; Besra is darker with a bold throat stripe and heavier barring; Shikra's pale grey back and fine rufous bars are distinctive.
animal.whereToSee: City parks, orchards and canal-side trees across Pakistan and India

lore: Shikras were trained for small-game hawking in Mughal and later Indian falconry, and the English word 'shikra' was taken directly from Hindustani.
funFact: A 2024 genetic study broke up the old genus Accipiter, and the Shikra was moved into the revived genus Tachyspiza.

otherNames: Zōng wěi hóng zhì 棕尾虹雉 (Chinese)
summary: A pheasant of high Himalayan meadows and forests whose male shimmers in metallic green, copper, purple and blue, crowned by a wiry crest of spatulate plumes. It is the national bird of Nepal.
nativeRange: Himalaya from eastern Afghanistan and northern Pakistan through India, Nepal and Bhutan to southern Tibet and NE India
abilities: Digs vigorously with its strong curved bill for roots, tubers and insect larvae, even through snow
Lives between about 2,100 and 4,500 m, moving downslope in winter
Male's plumage is iridescent structural colour that shifts with the angle of light

animal.diet: Tubers, roots, shoots, seeds, berries and invertebrates
animal.habitat: Oak, rhododendron and conifer forest with open grassy slopes and alpine meadows
animal.size: About 63–72 cm long; males up to about 2.4 kg
animal.behaviour: Feeds in loose groups on open slopes at dawn and dusk; when flushed it hurtles downhill with a ringing whistle.
fieldMarks: Male: iridescent green head, crest of spatula-tipped plumes, copper nape, purple-blue back
Male: conspicuous white rump and cinnamon-rufous tail in flight
Female: mottled brown with a white throat, bare blue skin around the eye and white-tipped tail
Heavy, curved bill used for digging
animal.voice: Loud, plaintive whistles 'kur-leiu' or 'kleeh-wick', often heard at dawn and when flushed
animal.lookalikes: Sclater's monal (eastern Himalaya) has a curly crest and white-tipped tail; Chinese monal (central China, outside its range) has a drooping purple crest rather than spatulate plumes; Koklass pheasant is streaked grey with a long dark ear-tuft.
animal.whereToSee: Kaghan and Neelum valleys and Ayubia in Pakistan; Tungnath-Chopta and Kedarnath in Uttarakhand; Sagarmatha and Langtang national parks in Nepal
animal.season: Resident; descends to lower forests in winter, easiest to see in spring and autumn

lore: As the Danphe it is Nepal's national bird and appears on Nepalese stamps; it is also the state bird of Uttarakhand. Men in Himachal Pradesh once wore the male's crest on their caps, a practice that drove hunting until legal protection.
funFact: The old English name 'Impeyan pheasant' and the species epithet honour Lady Mary Impey, who kept a menagerie in 18th-century Calcutta.

otherNames: Hēi tóu jiǎo zhì 黑头角雉 (Chinese)
summary: Perhaps the rarest pheasant of the western Himalaya, the male is black and crimson, spangled with white spots, and in display inflates a vivid blue-and-pink throat lappet and two fleshy blue horns. It lives in a narrow belt of temperate forest in Pakistan and India.
nativeRange: Western Himalaya: Kohistan and Kashmir in northern Pakistan, Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and western Uttarakhand in India
abilities: Male inflates a bib-like lappet of bare skin and erects fleshy 'horns' during courtship display
Survives on leaves, buds and seeds through snowy Himalayan winters
Unusually for a pheasant, often feeds and roosts in trees

animal.diet: Leaves, shoots, buds, seeds, acorns and some invertebrates
animal.habitat: Dense temperate and sub-alpine forest of oak, fir and rhododendron with thick undergrowth, about 1,750–3,600 m
animal.size: Males about 55–72 cm long (published figures vary)
animal.behaviour: Extremely shy and seldom seen; males call from steep, forested slopes in spring and display hidden from view.
fieldMarks: Male: black head and breast with crimson neck, the body covered in white, black-edged spots
Male: bare red facial skin, blue throat lappet and fleshy blue horns visible in display
Female: grey-brown, finely vermiculated and spotted with white
Heavy, short-tailed pheasant shape
animal.voice: A loud, wailing, goat-like 'waa-waa-oo-a', given mostly at dawn in spring
animal.lookalikes: Satyr tragopan (central and eastern Himalaya) is overall deep red with white spots and a red breast; the ranges barely meet, and the Western's black-and-grey body and crimson neck separate it.
animal.whereToSee: Great Himalayan National Park and Daranghati Sanctuary in Himachal Pradesh; Palas Valley in Kohistan, Pakistan
animal.season: Resident; males call April–June; moves lower in winter

lore: As the 'jujurana' it is the state bird of Himachal Pradesh, and a captive breeding programme at Sarahan in Himachal has bred the species since the 1990s.
funFact: The fleshy 'horns' that give tragopans their name (Greek for 'goat-Pan') are bare skin that the male erects only during display.

summary: A pale, long-tailed pheasant of steep grassy Himalayan slopes, buff-grey and heavily barred, with a long backward-pointing crest. Its dependence on scrubby grassland maintained by grazing and fire makes it unusual among Himalayan pheasants.
nativeRange: Western and central Himalaya from northern Pakistan (now very rare) through Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand to central Nepal
abilities: Lives on precipitous grass and scrub slopes most pheasants avoid
Digs for roots and tubers with its bill
Pairs and families call in loud chorus at dawn and dusk

animal.diet: Roots, tubers, seeds, grubs and insects
animal.habitat: Steep grassy slopes with scattered scrub and trees, roughly 1,200–3,000 m
animal.size: Males about 90–118 cm including the long tail
animal.behaviour: Coveys feed quietly in dense grass and are very hard to see; they call loudly at dawn and dusk and fly off downhill when disturbed.
fieldMarks: Pale buff and grey body barred and spotted with black
Very long, broadly barred, pointed tail
Long, wispy crest swept back from the crown
Bare red skin around the eye
animal.voice: A loud, ringing 'chir-a-pir, chir-a-pir, chir chir chirwa', given in duet or chorus at dawn and dusk
animal.lookalikes: Kalij pheasant is dark blue-black with a white rump; Koklass is greyer with a dark head and long ear-tufts; Cheer's pale barred plumage and very long tail are distinctive.
animal.whereToSee: Majathal Sanctuary and Chail in Himachal Pradesh; Dhorpatan Hunting Reserve in Nepal

lore: The scientific name honours Nathaniel Wallich, the Danish botanist who directed the Calcutta Botanic Garden in the early 19th century.
funFact: Unlike most pheasants, it seems to depend on grassland kept open by village grazing, grass-cutting and burning, so changes in traditional land use can harm it.

summary: A plump, grey and buff partridge of rocky hillsides, with a black necklace framing a creamy throat and bold black bars on its flanks. It is the national bird of Pakistan and a celebrated figure of Urdu and Punjabi poetry.
nativeRange: SE Europe and Turkey through the Middle East, Central Asia, Afghanistan, Pakistan and the western Himalaya to China and Mongolia; introduced in western North America, Hawaii and New Zealand
abilities: Runs uphill to escape, using wing-flapping to boost traction on steep slopes
Survives arid mountains by obtaining much of its water from green plants and insects
Introduced populations thrive in the dry ranges of the American West

animal.diet: Seeds, grasses, leaves, berries and insects
animal.habitat: Rocky, sparsely vegetated hills and mountain slopes, from near sea level to above 4,000 m
animal.behaviour: Coveys run up slopes rather than fly, then burst into the air and glide downhill on bowed wings; males call loudly from rocks.
fieldMarks: Grey-brown back and blue-grey breast
Creamy white throat and face bordered by a black band through the eye and around the throat
Bold black-and-chestnut bars on pale flanks
Red bill, red legs and red eye-ring
animal.voice: A loud, accelerating 'chuck-chuck-chukar-chukar', from which its name derives
animal.lookalikes: Rock partridge (SE Europe) has a white throat without buff tones; See-see partridge (Pakistan's low hills) is much smaller and sandy with no black necklace; Red-legged partridge (W Europe) has a streaked black necklace.
animal.whereToSee: Salt Range, Margalla Hills, Balochistan uplands and Gilgit-Baltistan in Pakistan; Ladakh and Spiti in India

lore: In Urdu, Punjabi and Hindi poetry the chakor is said to gaze at the moon all night and drink its light, a symbol of the lover's devoted longing. It is Pakistan's national bird, and chukars are traditionally kept and fought in the northwest.
funFact: Introduced to Nevada and other western US states for hunting, the chukar now thrives in rugged country where few native gamebirds live.

summary: A finely barred grey-brown partridge of dry plains whose loud, rhythmic calls ring across the farmlands of Pakistan and India at dawn. It is the 'teetar' of village life, long kept as a caged songbird and fighting bird in Punjab.
nativeRange: SE Iran and the Persian Gulf through Pakistan, India and Nepal's terai to Sri Lanka; introduced to the Andaman Islands, Hawaii and elsewhere
abilities: Thrives in arid scrub and cultivated plains with little cover
Males call in duet with neighbours to proclaim territory
Prefers running to flight, escaping through crop fields

animal.diet: Seeds, grain, shoots and insects such as termites and beetles
animal.habitat: Open dry plains, thorn scrub, farmland edges and semi-desert
animal.behaviour: Pairs and small coveys forage on the ground in early morning and late afternoon and roost in thorny trees and bushes at night.
fieldMarks: Grey-brown upperparts finely barred with buff and chestnut
Pale, densely cross-barred underparts
Rufous-buff throat bordered by a thin dark line
Chestnut outer tail feathers visible in flight
animal.voice: A loud, ringing, repeated 'ka-tee-tar, ka-tee-tar' or 'pateela-pateela', often accelerating; one of the defining dawn sounds of the Indus plains
animal.lookalikes: Black francolin male is black with a white cheek and chestnut collar; females of Black francolin have a chestnut patch on the hindneck; Painted francolin (central India) is spotted white on black.
animal.whereToSee: Common in dry farmland and scrub across Punjab and Sindh, Thar Desert fringes and peninsular India

lore: The calling teetar in a cane cage is a traditional sight in rural Punjab, and sayings about the bird recur in Punjabi and Urdu folk speech; teetar fighting was a widespread village pastime.
funFact: The species name pondicerianus refers to Pondicherry, the French colony in southern India from which early specimens reached Europe.

summary: A glossy black, fork-tailed bird that rides on grazing cattle and fearlessly dive-bombs crows, kites and eagles that come near its nest. Smaller birds often nest close to drongos for protection.
nativeRange: SE Iran and Afghanistan through Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh to southern China, Southeast Asia and Java; introduced to the Mariana Islands
abilities: Aggressively attacks much larger birds of prey and crows near its nest
Hawks flying insects stirred up by cattle, tractors and grass fires
Mimics the calls of other species, including the Shikra

animal.diet: Insects caught in the air or on the ground: grasshoppers, moths, termites, bees; occasionally small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Open farmland, grassland, roadsides and light woodland
animal.behaviour: Perches on wires, fence posts and the backs of buffalo and cattle, sallying out after insects; during the breeding season it will chase and strike raptors many times its size.
fieldMarks: All glossy blue-black plumage
Long, deeply forked tail with the outer tips flaring outward
Small white spot at the gape (corner of the bill) in adults
Upright posture on exposed perches
animal.voice: Harsh, varied 'ti-tiu' and 'cheece-cheece' calls; often one of the first birds to call before dawn
animal.lookalikes: Ashy drongo is slate-grey with a red eye; Bronzed and Racket-tailed drongos are forest birds, the latter with long wire-like tail rackets; male Asian koel is black but has a red eye and pale bill.
animal.whereToSee: Common over farmland across Pakistan and India, easily seen on livestock along the Indus and Ganges plains
animal.season: Mostly resident; northern populations (including much of Pakistan) partly migratory, more widespread in summer

lore: Its Hindi and Urdu name kotwal means the town's police chief, a nod to the way it patrols and chases off intruders.
funFact: Smaller birds such as bulbuls and orioles are known to nest close to drongo nests, apparently gaining protection from its aggressive defence.

summary: A small flycatcher whose adult male trails two ribbon-like tail feathers several times its body length, in either rufous or white with a glossy black crested head. Watching one float through a shady grove is among the classic sights of the South Asian monsoon.
nativeRange: Breeds from Turkestan and Afghanistan through northern Pakistan, the Himalaya and India to Sri Lanka and Bangladesh; northern birds winter in southern India and Sri Lanka
abilities: Male grows tail streamers that can add more than 20 cm to a body of about 20 cm
Catches insects in agile aerial sallies beneath the canopy
Males exist in two colour morphs, rufous and white

animal.diet: Flying insects: flies, moths, butterflies, beetles
animal.habitat: Shady deciduous woodland, groves, orchards and wooded gardens, often near water
animal.size: Body about 19–22 cm; male's streamers add up to about 24 cm
animal.behaviour: Both parents share incubation, including the long-tailed male, whose streamers hang over the side of the small cup nest.
fieldMarks: Glossy black head with short crest and blue eye-ring in both sexes
Adult male: very long central tail streamers, either chestnut-rufous or white
Female and young male: rufous back and tail, grey breast, no streamers
Small blue-grey bill
animal.voice: A harsh, grating 'chè' or 'chwè' call; a short, warbling song in the breeding season
animal.lookalikes: Amur paradise flycatcher (passage in NE India, SE Asia) has a darker grey throat and less contrasting hood; Blyth's paradise flycatcher (NE India to SE Asia) is very similar; the long tail separates males from all other South Asian flycatchers.
animal.whereToSee: Margalla Hills National Park near Islamabad and the Murree foothills in summer; Corbett, Pench and Kanha in India; widespread in Sri Lanka in winter
animal.season: Summer visitor to Pakistan and northern India (Apr–Sep); resident or winter visitor in the south

lore: It is the state bird of Madhya Pradesh, and the Urdu name shah bulbul ('king bulbul') reflects its regal tail.
funFact: Young males start out rufous like females, and some white males turn white only after several moults.

summary: A pied black-and-white bird that cocks its tail and sings sweet, varied songs from rooftops and garden trees at dawn. As the doel, it is the national bird of Bangladesh.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh and Myanmar through southern China to Southeast Asia
abilities: Rich, varied song that includes mimicry of other birds
Nests readily in wall holes and nest boxes in villages and towns
Males defend territories fiercely and sing through the hottest months

animal.diet: Insects and other invertebrates; occasionally small lizards, nectar and fruit
animal.habitat: Gardens, villages, open woodland and cultivation
animal.behaviour: Hops on the ground with tail cocked and fanned, flicking it up and down; males sing from exposed perches especially at dawn.
fieldMarks: Male: glossy blue-black head, breast and upperparts with a white belly
Bold white wing stripe and white outer tail feathers
Female: same pattern but grey where the male is black
Tail often cocked upright
animal.voice: Sweet, varied song of whistles and warbles, often with mimicry; scolding 'chrrr' alarm
animal.lookalikes: White-rumped shama has a long tail, orange belly and white rump; Pied bushchat is smaller with a short tail and no white tail sides; Indian robin male is black with a chestnut vent.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens in Dhaka, Kolkata and Colombo; Lahore's and Islamabad's leafy suburbs; widespread in Southeast Asian towns
animal.season: Resident year-round; most song from February to June

lore: The doel is Bangladesh's national bird and gives its name to Doel Chattar, a well-known monument in Dhaka. In Southeast Asia it was long trapped and kept for its song, causing declines in Singapore and parts of Indonesia.

otherNames: Yìndù bāsè dōng 印度八色鸫 (Chinese)
summary: A plump, short-tailed ground bird painted green, sky-blue, buff, black and scarlet, which hops on the forest floor turning over leaves. It migrates within the subcontinent, arriving in northern forests with the monsoon to breed.
nativeRange: Breeds in the Himalayan foothills (from NE Pakistan to Nepal), central and western India; winters in peninsular India and Sri Lanka
abilities: Migrates at night within South Asia and is sometimes found exhausted in towns
Flicks dead leaves aside with its bill to expose insects and worms
Builds a large domed nest of twigs and leaves on or near the ground

animal.diet: Insects, earthworms, snails and other ground invertebrates
animal.habitat: Deciduous and evergreen forest undergrowth, scrub jungle, well-vegetated gardens
animal.behaviour: Mostly silent and secretive, but calls loudly at dawn and dusk, often from a tree perch in the breeding season.
fieldMarks: Stocky, almost tailless bird with long legs
Bright green back, shining blue patch on the wing and rump
Buff underparts with a scarlet-crimson belly and vent
Bold black eye-stripe with white above, and a buff crown stripe
animal.voice: A loud, clear, two-note whistle 'wheet-tew', given mostly at dawn and dusk
animal.lookalikes: Hooded pitta (NE India, Southeast Asia) has a black head with a chestnut crown and no white supercilium; Blue-winged pitta has a darker head and more blue in the wing.
animal.whereToSee: Breeding forests of Uttarakhand, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra; wintering in Sri Lanka's dry zone and the Western Ghats; occasionally Margalla Hills, Pakistan
animal.season: Summer (monsoon) breeder in the north (May–Sep); winter visitor in the south and Sri Lanka (Oct–Apr)

lore: Its folk name navrang, 'nine colours', is used across north India for a bird whose plumage seems to hold every colour of the forest.
funFact: Migrating Indian pittas regularly turn up in cities in southern India and Sri Lanka after striking buildings during their night flights.

otherNames: Chì xiōng nǐ zhuómùniǎo 赤胸拟啄木鸟 (Chinese)
summary: A small green barbet with a crimson forehead and breast patch, whose monotonous metallic 'tuk-tuk-tuk' sounds like a coppersmith hammering a pot. It is a familiar fruit-eater of fig trees in towns from Pakistan to the Philippines.
nativeRange: Pakistan (Punjab and northwest), India, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh through Southeast Asia to the Philippines and the Greater Sundas
abilities: Disperses the seeds of figs and other fruiting trees
Excavates its own nest hole in soft, dead wood
Calls for long periods with the throat puffing out on each note

animal.diet: Mainly figs and other fruit; some insects
animal.habitat: Groves, gardens and open woodland with fig and other fruit trees
animal.behaviour: Often sits on a bare branch at the top of a tree in the morning sun, calling and bobbing its head left and right with each note.
fieldMarks: Small, chunky green barbet with a heavy bill
Crimson forehead and crimson patch on the upper breast
Yellow throat and yellow patches above and below the eye, separated by black
Pale underparts streaked with green
animal.voice: A loud, repetitive, metallic 'tuk… tuk… tuk', kept up for minutes, like a hammer on copper
animal.lookalikes: Brown-headed barbet is larger, brown-headed and streaked, with an orange eye-patch; Blue-throated barbet (Himalaya) has a blue face and throat.
animal.whereToSee: Fig and peepal trees in Lahore, Delhi, Kolkata and Colombo; Keoladeo National Park
animal.season: Resident; calls loudly from February to May

lore: Its English and Hindi names both describe the call; in north Indian towns its steady hammering is one of the signature sounds of the hot season.
funFact: When calling, each 'tuk' is accompanied by a visible bulging of the throat skin, while the bird swings its head so the sound seems to come from different directions.

summary: A modest grey hornbill with a black casque on its curved bill, common in groves, temples and city avenues across much of the subcontinent. Like other hornbills, the female walls herself inside a tree-hole nest while the male feeds her through a slit.
nativeRange: Indian subcontinent: eastern Pakistan, India and the Nepal terai, south of the Himalaya
abilities: Female seals the nest entrance with mud and droppings, leaving only a narrow slit
Disperses large seeds of figs and other fruit trees
Survives in city parks and avenues with old fig trees

animal.diet: Mainly fruit, especially figs; also insects, lizards and small birds
animal.habitat: Dry open woodland, groves, gardens and large trees in towns
animal.behaviour: Pairs and small parties fly between trees with flaps and glides; the female moults her flight feathers while sealed in the nest.
fieldMarks: Grey-brown overall, paler below
Curved dark bill with a pointed black casque
Long, graduated tail with a dark band and white tip
Pale eyebrow stripe
animal.voice: A shrill, squealing 'kee-kee-kee' and a kite-like scream
animal.lookalikes: Malabar grey hornbill (Western Ghats) lacks a casque and has a yellowish bill; Sri Lanka grey hornbill is endemic to Sri Lanka; larger Oriental pied hornbill is black and white.
animal.whereToSee: Old park and avenue trees in Lahore (e.g. Bagh-e-Jinnah); Delhi's ridge forests; Ranthambore and Keoladeo

lore: It is one of the few hornbills to live in large South Asian cities, and urban birdwatchers in Delhi and Lahore have tracked nesting pairs in old trees for years.
funFact: While she is sealed in, the female moults her flight feathers and depends entirely on the male to bring food.

summary: The tallest flying bird in the world, standing about 1.5–1.8 m, grey with a bare red head and upper neck. Pairs are famously faithful and duet with trumpeting calls in the wet farmlands of northern India.
nativeRange: Northern and central India, the Nepal terai, Myanmar, Cambodia, Vietnam and Laos, and northern Australia; extinct in Pakistan, Thailand (reintroduced) and much of Southeast Asia
abilities: Tallest flying bird alive
Pairs perform synchronised unison calls and leaping dances
Breeds in rice paddies and village ponds alongside farmers

animal.diet: Roots, tubers, grain, aquatic plants, insects, frogs, snails and small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Marshes, shallow wetlands, flooded fields and wet farmland
animal.size: Height about 1.5–1.8 m; wingspan about 2.2–2.5 m
animal.behaviour: Pairs stay together year-round and build a large mound nest of reeds in shallow water during the monsoon.
fieldMarks: Very tall, pale grey crane with long pink-red legs
Bare red skin on the head and upper neck; grey crown
Dark grey-green bill
White tertial feathers droop over the tail
animal.voice: Loud, far-carrying trumpeting; pairs give a unison call in which the male's long notes and the female's shorter notes interlock
animal.lookalikes: Common crane (winter visitor) is smaller with a black-and-white head and neck; Demoiselle crane is small with a black neck and white ear tufts; Brolga (Australia) has a red band only on the head and a dewlap.
animal.whereToSee: Farmland and wetlands of Uttar Pradesh (Etawah, Mainpuri), Keoladeo National Park and Gujarat's Kheda district; Lumbini in Nepal

lore: In the Ramayana, the sage Valmiki's first verse was provoked by grief at a hunter killing one of a pair of krauncha birds, often identified with the sarus. The sarus is the state bird of Uttar Pradesh and is widely protected by farmers who regard it as sacred.
funFact: Uttar Pradesh holds the largest population, and most of these cranes nest in farmland rather than protected areas.

summary: A snow-white crane with a red face and black wingtips that migrates from the Arctic tundra to wetlands in China. Its western flock, which wintered in India and Iran, has all but disappeared.
nativeRange: Breeds in Arctic Yakutia and western Siberia; the main population winters at Poyang Lake on the Yangtze in China; former wintering sites in Iran and India (Keoladeo)
abilities: Migrates around 5,000 km between Siberia and China
Digs for roots and tubers of aquatic plants in shallow water
Depends on very specific shallow wetlands, making it highly vulnerable

animal.diet: Roots, tubers and shoots of aquatic plants; also invertebrates and small animals in summer
animal.habitat: Open tundra wetlands in summer; shallow lakes and marshes in winter
animal.size: About 140 cm tall; wingspan about 210–230 cm
animal.behaviour: Feeds in shallow water by probing deep into the mud; more strictly aquatic than any other crane.
fieldMarks: All-white plumage with black primary feathers visible in flight
Bare brick-red skin on the face and forehead
Long reddish-pink legs and a long, slightly serrated bill
Juveniles are rusty-cinnamon
animal.voice: A soft, musical, flute-like 'koonk-koonk', unlike the harsh trumpeting of other cranes
animal.lookalikes: White stork has a red bill and black flight feathers along the whole rear wing; Great white egret and spoonbills are slimmer and lack a red face.
animal.whereToSee: Poyang Lake, Jiangxi, China, in winter; Momoge reserve in Jilin on migration
animal.season: Winter visitor to China (Nov–Mar); breeds in Siberia (May–Aug)

lore: Keoladeo (Bharatpur) in India was the famous wintering site of the western population until the last birds stopped arriving after 2002. The western flock's route passed through Afghanistan and Pakistan, where hunting took a heavy toll.
funFact: Nearly the entire world population, a few thousand birds, spends the winter at a single lake system in China.

summary: A tall, ostrich-like bustard, among the heaviest flying birds in the world, now reduced to fewer than 200 birds (including those in captivity), almost all in the Thar Desert of Rajasthan. Collision with overhead power lines is one of its biggest killers.
nativeRange: Formerly much of India and eastern Pakistan; now mainly Jaisalmer district, Rajasthan, with tiny remnants in Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka; possibly occasional in Cholistan, Pakistan
abilities: Males can weigh around 15 kg, among the heaviest flying birds
In display, the male inflates a large throat pouch and cocks his tail, booming
Lays a single egg on bare ground

animal.diet: Grasshoppers, beetles, small lizards and rodents; also seeds, berries and shoots
animal.habitat: Arid and semi-arid grassland with scattered scrub
animal.size: About 1 m tall; males up to about 15 kg
animal.behaviour: Walks slowly through grassland; its forward-facing eyes and poor manoeuvrability in flight make it unable to avoid power lines.
fieldMarks: Very large, long-legged bird with a horizontal body
Black crown and crest on a white head and neck
Brown back and wings; males have a black breast band
Black-and-white wing pattern in flight
animal.voice: A deep, booming 'hoonk' carried a long way, given by displaying males
animal.lookalikes: Macqueen's (houbara) bustard is much smaller and sandy with a black neck stripe; Lesser florican is small with long head plumes in breeding males.
animal.whereToSee: Desert National Park near Jaisalmer, Rajasthan (with permits)
animal.season: Resident; displays mainly during the monsoon

lore: The ornithologist Salim Ali proposed it as India's national bird. It is the state bird of Rajasthan, and India's Supreme Court has heard cases on burying or marking power lines in its habitat.
funFact: A captive breeding centre at Jaisalmer has hatched dozens of chicks since 2019 as insurance against extinction.

summary: A large cliff-nesting vulture of India and Pakistan that once swarmed over every carcass. From the 1990s its numbers crashed by more than 95%, poisoned by the veterinary drug diclofenac in the cattle carcasses it ate.
nativeRange: Central and peninsular India and SE Pakistan (Sindh, notably Nagarparkar)
abilities: Clears carcasses rapidly, reducing disease and feral dog populations
Soars for hours on thermals, scanning for food
Nests on cliffs and old buildings in colonies

animal.diet: Carrion, especially dead cattle
animal.habitat: Open country near villages and cliffs; dry hilly regions
animal.size: About 80–100 cm long; wingspan about 2 m
animal.behaviour: Groups descend on a carcass and can strip it in under an hour; they nest colonially on cliff ledges.
fieldMarks: Large pale sandy-brown vulture with dark flight feathers
Bare dark grey head and neck; white neck ruff
Pale yellowish bill
Long, broad wings held flat in soaring
animal.voice: Mostly silent; hisses and grunts at carcasses
animal.lookalikes: Slender-billed vulture (north India, Nepal) is darker with a thin dark bill and nests in trees; White-rumped vulture is darker with a white back patch; Eurasian griffon is larger and more rufous.
animal.whereToSee: Cliffs of Ranthambore, Orchha and Panna in India; Nagarparkar's Karoonjhar hills in Sindh

lore: Its collapse led India, Pakistan and Nepal to ban veterinary diclofenac in 2006, and the Parsi tradition of exposing the dead at Towers of Silence in Mumbai has been disrupted by the loss of vultures.
funFact: Researchers estimate the vulture collapse in India allowed rotting carcasses and feral dogs to increase, with a measurable rise in human deaths.

summary: A large white stork with a waxy yellow bill, a bare orange face and rose-pink feathers on its back, nesting in noisy colonies in wetland trees and even village trees. Its numbers have recovered enough that it was moved from Near Threatened to Least Concern in 2023.
nativeRange: Pakistan (Sindh) and India through Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh to Southeast Asia and southern China
abilities: Feels for fish by sweeping its half-open bill through water, snapping it shut in milliseconds
Nests in large mixed colonies alongside herons, cormorants and pelicans
Cools itself and its chicks by panting and shading them with spread wings

animal.diet: Mainly fish, also frogs, crustaceans and snakes
animal.habitat: Freshwater marshes, lakes, rice fields and reservoirs
animal.size: About 93–102 cm long; wingspan about 150–160 cm
animal.behaviour: Wades in shallow water with its bill submerged and partly open, moving it side to side and stirring the water with one foot.
fieldMarks: Large white stork with long, heavy, slightly down-curved yellow bill
Bare orange-red face
Black-and-white wings and black band across the breast
Pink-tinged tertials on the back; pinkish legs
animal.voice: Mostly silent; adults clatter their bills at the nest; chicks give loud begging calls
animal.lookalikes: Asian openbill is smaller, greyish, with a gap in its bill; Woolly-necked stork is dark with a white neck; Black-headed ibis has a black head and curved black bill.
animal.whereToSee: Keoladeo National Park (Bharatpur), Kokkare Bellur village in Karnataka and Ranganathittu
animal.season: Resident with local movements; breeds after the monsoon (Aug–Mar)

lore: At Kokkare Bellur in Karnataka, villagers have long protected the painted storks and pelicans that nest in their trees, using the droppings as fertiliser.
funFact: Its bill-sweeping strike is a touch reflex: it can catch fish in muddy water it cannot see through.

summary: A tall, striking stork with a glossy black neck that flashes green and purple, a massive black bill and coral-red legs. It is one of the few storks in which males and females can be told apart by eye colour.
nativeRange: India, Nepal and Sri Lanka through Southeast Asia to New Guinea and northern and eastern Australia
abilities: Hunts large prey including fish, turtles and snakes
Pairs defend large territories in wetlands
Performs a wing-spreading and bill-clattering greeting display at the nest

animal.diet: Fish, frogs, turtles, snakes, crustaceans and occasionally birds
animal.habitat: Freshwater marshes, river banks, lakes and flooded fields
animal.size: About 130–150 cm tall; wingspan about 2.3 m
animal.behaviour: Stalks slowly through shallow water and stabs prey with its huge bill; pairs nest alone in tall trees rather than in colonies.
fieldMarks: Very tall black-and-white stork
Glossy black head and neck with green and purple sheen
Massive, straight black bill
Bright coral-red legs; female has a yellow iris, male dark brown
animal.voice: Generally silent; bill-clattering at the nest
animal.lookalikes: Lesser adjutant is grey with a bare head; Woolly-necked stork has a white neck; Saddle-billed stork is African.
animal.whereToSee: Keoladeo National Park and the wetlands of Uttar Pradesh in India; Chitwan and Koshi Tappu in Nepal; Kakadu in Australia

lore: Australians long called it the jabiru, a name borrowed from a quite different South American stork.
funFact: The female's yellow iris is one of the easiest ways to sex any large bird in the field.

summary: A large, scaly-brown dabbling duck of South Asian wetlands, easily known by the yellow tip of its dark bill and a red spot at the bill's base. It is one of the few ducks resident and breeding across the plains of the subcontinent.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh and Myanmar
abilities: Breeds in the monsoon in small, vegetated wetlands
Upends to feed on submerged plants
Feeds at night in rice fields

animal.diet: Aquatic plants, seeds, grain and invertebrates
animal.habitat: Freshwater lakes, marshes, village ponds and rice fields
animal.behaviour: Usually in pairs or small groups; ducklings are hidden in dense reeds by the female.
fieldMarks: Large brown duck with a heavily scaled, spotted body
Dark bill with a bright yellow tip
Red spot on the face at the base of the bill (on the Indian form)
Pale head with a dark cap and eye-stripe; green speculum bordered white; white tertials
animal.voice: Female a loud quacking similar to a Mallard; male a softer, raspy note
animal.lookalikes: Eastern spot-billed duck (East Asia) lacks the red loral spot and has darker body plumage; female Mallard has an orange-and-dark bill and no yellow tip.
animal.whereToSee: Keoladeo National Park; Haleji and Keenjhar lakes in Sindh; wetlands of Sri Lanka

funFact: The red spot near the bill base is the main field mark separating it from its close East Asian relative, the Eastern spot-billed duck.

summary: An elegant wetland bird that walks across lotus and water-lily leaves on enormously long toes, its breeding plumage chocolate and white with a golden nape and a long, curving pheasant-like tail. Females are polyandrous, mating with several males that each raise a clutch alone.
nativeRange: Pakistan and India through Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Southeast Asia to southern China and Taiwan; northern birds migrate
abilities: Spreads its weight over very long toes to walk on floating leaves
Females lay eggs for several males, which incubate and rear the young
Males can carry eggs or chicks under their wings to move them

animal.diet: Insects, snails and other invertebrates, and seeds of aquatic plants
animal.habitat: Lakes, ponds and marshes with floating vegetation such as lotus and water lilies
animal.size: About 39–58 cm in breeding plumage including tail
animal.behaviour: The female defends a territory containing several males' nests; each male incubates eggs on a floating nest.
fieldMarks: Breeding: chocolate-brown body, white face and neck, golden-yellow hindneck, long dark sickle tail
Mostly white wings, very conspicuous in flight
Non-breeding: brown above, white below, with a dark breast band and no long tail
Very long legs and toes
animal.voice: A nasal, mewing 'me-onp' or 'tewn', often given in the breeding season
animal.lookalikes: Bronze-winged jacana is dark glossy with a white eyebrow and short tail; non-breeding birds may recall a large wader but the toes and white wings are distinctive.
animal.whereToSee: Keoladeo National Park; lotus lakes in Sindh (Haleji) and Bangladesh's haors; Taiwan's Guantian reserve
animal.season: Resident in South Asia; breeding plumage during the monsoon (Jun–Sep)

lore: In Taiwan, a dedicated reserve for this species was created at Guantian after a high-speed rail line threatened its breeding wetlands.
funFact: It is the only jacana that is a long-distance migrant, with northern birds from China moving south for the winter.

otherNames: Huáng xiōng zhī què 黄胸织雀 (Chinese)
summary: A sparrow-sized weaver whose breeding males stitch long, retort-shaped hanging nests from strips of green grass and palm leaf, often over water. Females inspect the half-built nests and choose a mate by the quality of his work.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh through Myanmar and Thailand to Sumatra and Java
abilities: Weaves nests with knots and loops from strips of grass torn from living leaves
Builds a long entrance tube that deters snakes and other predators
Males build several nests in a season and court females at each
Presses blobs of mud inside the nest chamber, possibly to balance it in wind

animal.diet: Seeds and grain, especially rice; insects for nestlings
animal.habitat: Cultivation, grassland and scrub with palms, acacias or trees near water
animal.behaviour: Colonies of nests hang from date and palmyra palms, thorny acacias and telephone wires; males flutter their wings and call at nests to attract females.
fieldMarks: Breeding male: bright yellow crown and breast patch, dark brown face mask and throat
Female and non-breeding male: streaked brown, sparrow-like, with a buff eyebrow
Heavy conical bill
Hanging retort-shaped nest is the easiest sign of the species
animal.voice: Chattering 'chit-chit' calls and a wheezy, sizzling song from males at the nest
animal.lookalikes: Black-breasted weaver has a black breast band; Streaked weaver has a heavily streaked breast; female resembles a House sparrow but has a heavier bill and streaked crown.
animal.whereToSee: Rice and sugarcane country across Punjab, Sindh and India; nests easily seen at Keoladeo and in Kerala and Sri Lankan paddy-lands
animal.season: Resident; colonies active during the monsoon (May–Sep)

lore: The Bengali poet Rajanikanta Sen's poem 'Swadhinatar Sukh' contrasts the babui weaver in its handmade nest with a sparrow sheltering in a borrowed house, a poem learned by schoolchildren in Bangladesh and West Bengal.
funFact: A folk belief holds that the bird sticks fireflies into the mud inside its nest to light it; the mud blobs are real, but the fireflies are not.

otherNames: Cháng wěi féng yè yīng 长尾缝叶莺 (Chinese)
summary: A tiny green warbler with a rusty cap and a cocked tail that literally sews its nest, piercing the edges of large leaves with its bill and stitching them into a cup with spider silk or plant fibre. Its loud call belies its size.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh to southern China, Southeast Asia and Java
abilities: Punches holes along a leaf margin and pulls fibres through, knotting them like rivets
Builds the nest inside one or more living leaves so it stays green and camouflaged
Thrives in city gardens and potted plants

animal.diet: Small insects, larvae and spiders
animal.habitat: Gardens, hedges, scrub, plantations and forest edge
animal.size: About 10–14 cm long; breeding males have longer central tail feathers
animal.behaviour: Restless, moving through low bushes with its tail cocked and flicking; the stitched leaf-cradle holds a soft cup of plant down.
fieldMarks: Tiny bright olive-green warbler with whitish underparts
Rufous forecrown
Long, thin, slightly curved bill
Long tail held upright, sometimes with dark spots near the base of the throat
animal.voice: A loud, repeated 'towit-towit-towit' or 'cheeyup-cheeyup', surprisingly loud for the bird's size
animal.lookalikes: Dark-necked tailorbird (NE India, SE Asia) has a dark throat patch; prinias are browner with long graduated tails and lack the rufous cap.
animal.whereToSee: Garden hedges and shrubs throughout Pakistan and India, e.g. Lahore, Karachi, Delhi and Colombo

lore: Rudyard Kipling's 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi' features Darzee and his wife, a pair of tailorbirds, named with the Hindustani word for tailor.
funFact: The 'stitches' are not true sewing: the fibres are pushed through each hole and fluffed out on the outside so they hold like a rivet.

summary: A scruffy grey-brown babbler that lives in noisy gangs of about seven to ten, hopping through leaf litter and squabbling constantly. Families defend territories together and help raise each other's young.
nativeRange: Pakistan (Indus plains), India, Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh
abilities: Cooperative breeder: helpers feed chicks that are not their own
Groups post a sentinel who watches for predators while others feed
Mobs snakes, cats and birds of prey as a group
Hosts brood parasites such as the Jacobin cuckoo and Common hawk-cuckoo

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, small lizards, seeds, nectar and fruit
animal.habitat: Woodland, scrub, gardens and cultivation edges
animal.behaviour: Groups move through low cover in a straggling procession, hopping on the ground and flipping leaves; members preen each other and huddle together on branches.
fieldMarks: Grey-brown with faint streaking, rather untidy-looking
Pale creamy-yellow iris and pale yellowish bill
Long, loose tail and short rounded wings
Always in noisy groups
animal.voice: Harsh, continual chattering and mewing 'ke-ke-ke' from the whole group
animal.lookalikes: Yellow-billed babbler (S India, Sri Lanka) has a paler head; Large grey babbler has white outer tail feathers; Common babbler is smaller and more streaked, in drier country.
animal.whereToSee: Parks and wooded gardens across India, e.g. Delhi's Lodhi Garden and Keoladeo; also Koshi Tappu in lowland Nepal

lore: Across north India and Bengal it is known as 'seven brothers' (or 'seven sisters' in English), after its habit of moving in squabbling family groups.

otherNames: Ròu chuí mài jī 肉垂麦鸡 (Chinese)
summary: A tall plover with a black cap, white face patch and a red fleshy wattle in front of each eye, whose frantic 'did-he-do-it' calls raise the alarm across South Asian fields, at all hours. It nests on bare ground and even on flat city rooftops.
nativeRange: Iraq and the Persian Gulf through Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh to Southeast Asia
abilities: Alerts the whole countryside to approaching people and predators with loud calls
Parents dive-bomb intruders and perform broken-wing distraction displays
Soaks belly feathers to carry water to eggs and chicks in great heat

animal.diet: Insects, snails, worms and other invertebrates
animal.habitat: Open ground near water: field edges, riverbanks, dry lake beds, lawns
animal.behaviour: Lays its well-camouflaged eggs in a shallow scrape on open ground; the chicks can run and feed themselves within hours of hatching.
fieldMarks: Black cap, throat and breast with white cheek patch running down to the white belly
Small red fleshy wattle in front of the eye; red bill with black tip
Pale brown back; long yellow legs
Broad white wingbar and black-and-white tail in flight
animal.voice: Loud, shrill 'did-he-do-it, did-he-do-it' or 'pity-to-do-it', often given in flight and at night
animal.lookalikes: Yellow-wattled lapwing has yellow wattles and yellow legs and lives in drier country; White-tailed lapwing (winter) has a plain grey-brown head and white tail; Sociable lapwing (rare winter visitor to Pakistan and India) has a black cap with white eyebrow.
animal.whereToSee: Field edges and canals throughout Punjab and Sindh; city parks in Lahore, Delhi and Colombo

lore: A widespread South Asian folk tale says the titeeri sleeps on its back with its legs in the air, ready to hold up the sky if it should fall; its Tamil name means 'the one that points out people', after its alarm call.

otherNames: Hè chì yā juān 褐翅鸦鹃 (Chinese)
summary: A large, crow-sized cuckoo with glossy black body, chestnut wings and a ruby-red eye, which clambers through hedges and stalks the ground for snakes and snails. Unlike many cuckoos, it builds its own nest and raises its own young.
nativeRange: Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh through southern China to Southeast Asia and the Greater Sundas
abilities: Hunts snakes, lizards, large insects, eggs and nestlings
Builds a domed nest of grass and leaves in dense cover
Flies weakly, preferring to clamber and run through vegetation

animal.diet: Large insects, snails, lizards, small snakes, frogs, eggs and nestlings; some fruit
animal.habitat: Dense scrub, hedges, reedbeds, gardens and forest edge
animal.behaviour: Walks deliberately through undergrowth and along field edges; suns itself with wings spread on bushes after rain.
fieldMarks: Glossy black head, body and long tail
Rich chestnut wings and back
Deep red eye
Heavy black bill
animal.voice: A deep, resonant, booming 'coop-coop-coop', often in long series and duetting between pairs
animal.lookalikes: Lesser coucal is smaller with buff streaks on the back; male Asian koel is all black with a pale bill; crows lack the chestnut wings.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens and hedgerows across India and Sri Lanka; canal banks and wooded areas of northern Punjab

lore: British sportsmen in India called it the 'crow pheasant', a name still found in older Indian bird books.
funFact: Despite being a cuckoo, it is not a brood parasite: both parents build the nest and feed the chicks.

otherNames: Héng bān fù xiǎo xiāo 横斑腹小鸮 (Chinese)
summary: A small, white-spotted owl with staring yellow eyes that lives in pairs and family groups in old trees, ruins and buildings across South Asia. It bobs its head comically when curious and chatters loudly at dusk.
nativeRange: Southern Iran through Pakistan, India, Nepal and Bangladesh to Myanmar and Indochina (absent from Sri Lanka)
abilities: Hunts beetles, moths and rodents around street lights and villages
Nests in tree holes, wall crevices and old buildings
Active at dusk and sometimes by day

animal.diet: Large insects, rodents, lizards and small birds
animal.habitat: Open country, villages, towns, groves and ruins
animal.behaviour: Pairs and families sit huddled together in a tree hole entrance by day and become noisy and active at dusk.
fieldMarks: Small, round-headed owl without ear-tufts
Grey-brown upperparts heavily spotted with white
White underparts barred with brown
Large yellow eyes with white eyebrows and a white collar
animal.voice: Harsh, screeching, chattering 'chirurr-chirurr-chirurr' and 'cheevak, cheevak', usually from pairs or groups
animal.lookalikes: Jungle owlet is barred (not spotted) on the head and back; Little owl (northern Pakistan) is browner with less spotting below; Collared scops owl has ear-tufts and dark eyes.
animal.whereToSee: Old trees and ruins in Lahore, Delhi, Agra and Karachi; farmland canals across Punjab

lore: In Hindu tradition the owl (uluka) is the vahana of the goddess Lakshmi, yet owls including this species are illegally trapped and sacrificed for black-magic rituals around Diwali, a trade documented by TRAFFIC India.

summary: The drake is one of the most ornate birds in the world, with orange 'whiskers', a pair of upright orange sail feathers on its back, and a purple breast bordered by white bars. A symbol of married love in China, Korea and Japan, it nests in tree holes high above the ground.
nativeRange: Russian Far East, NE China, Korea and Japan, wintering in eastern and southern China, Korea and Japan; feral populations in Britain and elsewhere in Europe
abilities: Nests in tree cavities up to 10 m or more above ground
Ducklings leap from the nest hole to the ground within a day of hatching, unharmed
Feeds on acorns and other nuts, unusual for a duck

animal.diet: Acorns, chestnuts, seeds, aquatic plants, insects and snails
animal.habitat: Wooded ponds, rivers and lakes with overhanging trees
animal.behaviour: Males court females in groups with ritual displays of crest-raising, mock drinking and preening behind the sail feathers.
fieldMarks: Drake: red bill, white crescent over the eye, orange cheek 'whiskers', upright orange sail feathers
Drake: purple breast with two white-and-black vertical bars; golden flanks
Female: grey with a white eye-ring and stripe behind the eye, white-spotted flanks
Small, crested duck that perches in trees
animal.voice: Generally quiet; males give a sharp whistle, females a soft clucking
animal.lookalikes: Wood duck (North America; escapees elsewhere) male is green-headed without sails; female Wood duck has a larger white teardrop eye patch and no pale stripe behind it.
animal.whereToSee: Ponds of Tokyo's Shinjuku Gyoen in winter, Seoul's Changgyeonggung Palace (Chundangji pond), Beijing's Summer Palace; feral in Virginia Water, England
animal.season: Resident in Japan; migratory in mainland Asia, wintering Oct–Mar in southern China and Korea

lore: In Chinese the pair 鸳鸯 (yuānyāng) means 'devoted lovers', and mandarin duck carvings are traditional wedding gifts in China and Korea. In fact, pairs usually form anew each winter.
funFact: In summer the drake moults into a drab, female-like eclipse plumage, still identifiable by its red bill.

otherNames: Rì fēi xiù yǎn niǎo 日菲绣眼鸟 (Chinese)
summary: A small yellow-green bird with a crisp white ring around each eye, a lively flocking visitor to flowering camellias and plum blossom in Japanese winter gardens. It is a major pollinator of camellias in its native range.
nativeRange: Japan (including the Ryukyu and Ogasawara islands) and South Korea; populations in the Philippines and Indonesia formerly called Mountain white-eye; introduced to Hawaii
abilities: Pollinates camellias and other winter flowers by feeding on their nectar
Flocks huddle tightly side by side on branches
Brush-tipped tongue laps nectar

animal.diet: Nectar, fruit and small insects
animal.habitat: Broadleaf forest, parks, orchards and gardens
animal.behaviour: Moves in active groups through blossom, hanging upside down to reach flowers; in winter flocks roost pressed close together.
fieldMarks: Small olive-green bird with a bright yellow throat
Bold white eye-ring
Pale greyish-white belly
Thin, slightly curved, pointed bill
animal.voice: A thin, high 'chii' contact call; song is a fast, twittering warble
animal.lookalikes: Swinhoe's white-eye (China, Taiwan, SE Asia) has paler flanks and a smaller yellow throat; Chestnut-flanked white-eye has rufous flanks; Japanese bush warbler is drabber with no eye-ring.
animal.whereToSee: Plum and cherry gardens in Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka in winter and spring; Jeju Island in Korea
animal.season: Resident year-round; most conspicuous in winter at flowers

lore: The Japanese expression mejiro-oshi ('white-eye pushing') describes people crowded together, after the way these birds line up shoulder to shoulder on a branch. Mejiro paired with plum blossom is a classic motif in Japanese painting.
funFact: Many Japanese think of the green bird at plum blossom as the uguisu (bush warbler), but the bird most often seen there is the mejiro; the real uguisu is drab and secretive.

otherNames: Dōngfāng bái guàn 东方白鹳 (Chinese)
summary: A large white stork with black flight feathers and a heavy black bill, breeding in the Amur basin and wintering along the Yangtze. It went extinct in the wild in Japan in 1971 and has been brought back through reintroduction at Toyooka.
nativeRange: Breeds in the Amur and Ussuri basins of the Russian Far East and NE China; winters mainly in the Yangtze basin, with smaller numbers in Korea, Japan and Taiwan
abilities: Migrates between the Russian Far East and the Yangtze floodplain
Nests on tall trees and electricity pylons
Communicates by loud bill-clattering, being almost voiceless

animal.diet: Fish, frogs, snakes, crustaceans and insects
animal.habitat: Wetlands, river floodplains, rice paddies and lake margins
animal.size: About 110–128 cm long; wingspan about 2.1 m
animal.behaviour: Feeds by walking slowly through shallow water; in Japan, reintroduced storks forage in rice paddies managed without pesticides.
fieldMarks: Large white stork with black flight feathers
Heavy, black bill (red in White stork)
Red bare skin around a whitish eye
Red legs
animal.voice: Almost silent; loud bill-clattering at the nest
animal.lookalikes: White stork (Europe, Central Asia) is smaller with a red bill; Black-faced spoonbill and egrets are smaller with different bills.
animal.whereToSee: Poyang Lake and Dongting Lake in China in winter; Toyooka, Hyogo Prefecture, Japan year-round
animal.season: Winter visitor to the Yangtze (Nov–Mar); summer visitor to the breeding grounds; resident in reintroduced Japanese populations

lore: In Japan, as in Europe, the stork came to be linked with bringing babies. Toyooka city began releasing captive-bred storks in 2005, promoting 'stork-friendly' pesticide-reduced rice as part of the recovery.
funFact: Wild storks bred in Japan again in 2007, the first wild-hatched chick in the country in over four decades.

summary: A white ibis blushed with salmon-pink, with a shaggy nape crest and a bare red face, that came within seven birds of extinction. From a handful found in Shaanxi in 1981, careful protection has rebuilt a population of thousands.
nativeRange: Formerly Japan, Korea, eastern China and the Russian Far East; now wild mainly in Shaanxi province, China, with reintroduced populations on Sado Island (Japan) and in South Korea
abilities: Probes rice paddies and streams for loaches, frogs and invertebrates
Smears a dark secretion from its neck onto its plumage, turning it grey in the breeding season
Recovered from a wild population of seven birds

animal.diet: Small fish, loaches, frogs, crabs, snails and insects
animal.habitat: Rice paddies, streams and wetlands near tall trees used for nesting and roosting
animal.behaviour: Feeds by probing its long curved bill into mud and water; nests in tall trees on wooded slopes near paddies.
fieldMarks: White plumage with a salmon-pink flush to the wings and tail, strongest underneath in flight
Bare red face and red legs
Long, down-curved black bill with red tip
Shaggy crest at the back of the head; grey head and back in breeding season
animal.voice: A harsh, crow-like 'aaa' call
animal.lookalikes: Black-headed ibis has a black head and neck and lacks the pink; spoonbills have a flat, spoon-shaped bill; egrets have straight bills.
animal.whereToSee: Yangxian County, Shaanxi, China; Sado Island, Niigata Prefecture, Japan

lore: The toki gave its colour name 'toki-iro' (a soft pink) to Japanese, and it is the symbol of Niigata Prefecture. Japan's last native-born crested ibis, Kin, died in 2003, and the species was reintroduced to Sado from Chinese stock in 2008.
funFact: Its genus name Nipponia and species name nippon both mean 'Japan', making it one of the most emphatically Japanese names in zoology.

summary: One of the largest and most powerful eagles in the world, with a shaggy crest, a huge arched blue-grey bill and pale blue eyes. Found only in the rainforests of the Philippines, it is the national bird and among the rarest raptors on Earth.
nativeRange: Endemic to the Philippines: Mindanao, Luzon, Samar and Leyte
abilities: Hunts flying lemurs (colugos), monkeys, civets and large birds in the forest canopy
Pairs hunt cooperatively, one distracting a monkey troop while the other strikes
Raises a single chick every two years

animal.diet: Colugos (Philippine flying lemurs), macaques, palm civets, flying squirrels, hornbills, snakes
animal.habitat: Primary dipterocarp forest on steep mountain slopes
animal.size: About 86–102 cm long; wingspan about 1.8–2.2 m
animal.behaviour: Hunts by perching in the canopy and moving between trees, then flying fast through the forest to seize prey with its massive talons.
fieldMarks: Very large eagle with a shaggy, spiky crest
Huge, deeply arched blue-grey bill
Dark face, brown upperparts, cream-white underparts
Pale blue-grey eyes; broad, short wings and long tail
animal.voice: High-pitched whistles, rising at the end, especially from young birds begging
animal.lookalikes: Changeable hawk-eagle and Philippine hawk-eagle are much smaller with less massive bills; no other Philippine raptor approaches its size.
animal.whereToSee: Philippine Eagle Center near Davao City; Mount Kitanglad and Mount Apo, Mindanao

lore: Proclaimed the national bird of the Philippines in 1995, it gave its Filipino name Haribon ('king of birds') to the country's leading conservation society. The first captive-bred chick, Pag-asa ('hope'), hatched in 1992.
funFact: Despite its old name 'monkey-eating eagle', its main prey on Mindanao is the colugo, a gliding mammal.

otherNames: Dà yǎn bān zhì 大眼斑雉 (Chinese)
summary: A huge, secretive pheasant of Sundaic rainforest whose male has enormous wing feathers covered with rows of shaded eyespots, which he fans into a great circular screen during display. Charles Darwin wrote at length about the eyespots as evidence for sexual selection.
nativeRange: Malay Peninsula (southern Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia), Sumatra and Borneo
abilities: Male clears a 'dancing ground' on the forest floor of leaves and debris
Fans its huge secondary feathers into an upright disc displaying hundreds of eyespots
Eyespots are shaded so they appear three-dimensional, like balls in sockets

animal.diet: Fallen fruit, seeds, leaves, ants and other invertebrates
animal.habitat: Lowland and hill dipterocarp rainforest
animal.size: Males up to about 1.6–2 m including the tail; females about 75 cm
animal.behaviour: Males call from their dancing grounds and display there to visiting females; the species is far more often heard than seen.
fieldMarks: Very large pheasant with a small bare blue head
Male: extremely long central tail feathers and broad secondaries with rows of eyespots
Overall brown, finely patterned plumage
Female much smaller with a short tail
animal.voice: Loud, far-carrying 'kwow-wow' calls from males, and a long series of 'wow' notes that accelerate; one of the classic sounds of Malaysian forests
animal.lookalikes: Crested argus (Vietnam, Laos, Malaysia's highlands) has a crest and different eyespot pattern; peacock-pheasants are much smaller with metallic eyespots.
animal.whereToSee: Taman Negara, Malaysia; Danum Valley, Sabah; Khao Sok and Hala-Bala in Thailand

lore: Named after Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed giant of Greek myth. In 'The Descent of Man' (1871), Darwin used the gradation of the great argus's eyespots to argue how sexual selection could build complex ornaments step by step.
funFact: The male's display is so rarely witnessed in the wild that much of what is known comes from captive birds and camera traps.

summary: A huge black-and-white hornbill crowned with an extravagant upturned orange-red casque, like a rhinoceros horn. It is the state bird of Sarawak, 'Land of the Hornbills', and a major disperser of rainforest seeds.
nativeRange: Southern Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra, Java and Borneo; long extinct as a breeder in Singapore, with occasional wild wanderers recorded since 2025
abilities: Disperses the large seeds of figs and other rainforest trees over wide areas
Female seals herself into a tree cavity nest, fed by the male
Wingbeats are so loud they can be heard from a distance as a whooshing roar

animal.diet: Mainly figs and other fruit; also insects, lizards and small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Lowland and hill rainforest with large old trees
animal.behaviour: Pairs fly between fruiting trees with loud, whooshing wingbeats; the sealed-in female relies on the male for months.
fieldMarks: Very large black hornbill with white belly and white tail with a black band
Massive ivory-yellow bill topped by an orange-red casque curving upward like a horn
Red eye in males, white eye in females
Loud wing noise in flight
animal.voice: Deep, resonant 'gronk' calls; pairs duet with the male's lower notes and the female's higher ones
animal.lookalikes: Great hornbill has a flatter, yellow, two-pointed casque and a white neck; Helmeted hornbill has a short red casque and long central tail feathers.
animal.whereToSee: Taman Negara (Malaysia), Kinabatangan River and Danum Valley (Sabah), Lambir Hills (Sarawak), Khao Sok (Thailand)

lore: Among the Iban of Sarawak, the kenyalang is the messenger of the upper world, and carved hornbill effigies were raised in the Gawai Kenyalang festival. The bird appears on Sarawak's coat of arms.
funFact: Its casque is mostly hollow and light, unlike the solid casque of the Helmeted hornbill.

summary: A tall, upright peafowl clad in shimmering green and bronze scales with a narrow tuft-like crest, the Southeast Asian counterpart of the Indian peafowl. Both sexes are brightly coloured, and the male carries a glittering train of eyespot feathers.
nativeRange: Formerly NE India and Bangladesh to Southeast Asia and Java; now in fragmented populations in Yunnan (China), Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam and Java
abilities: Males raise a train of over 100 eyespotted feathers in display
Roosts high in trees and calls loudly at dawn and dusk
Can fly strongly despite its size

animal.diet: Seeds, grain, fruit, insects, small reptiles and frogs
animal.habitat: Open forest, riverbanks and forest edges with grassy clearings
animal.size: Males about 1.8–3 m including the train; females about 1–1.1 m
