animal.behaviour: Feeds in clearings and on riverbanks in early morning and evening, retreating to dense cover; males display at traditional sites.
fieldMarks: Upright, slim crest of tufts (not fan-shaped as in Indian peafowl)
Green and bronze scaly neck and breast (not blue)
Bare yellow-and-blue facial skin
Females almost as colourful as males, but without the train
animal.voice: Loud, honking 'ki-wao' or 'aow-aaw', less shrill than the Indian peafowl
animal.lookalikes: Indian peafowl male has a blue neck and fan-shaped crest, and the female is drab brown; hybrids ('Spalding' peafowl) occur in captivity.
animal.whereToSee: Huai Kha Khaeng Wildlife Sanctuary (Thailand), Baluran National Park (Java), Cat Tien (Vietnam), and parts of Yunnan
animal.season: Resident year-round; breeding display in the dry season

lore: The peacock was the emblem of the Burmese Konbaung kings and remains a national symbol of Myanmar.
funFact: A 2016 survey estimated fewer than 500 wild green peafowl left in China, all in Yunnan.

summary: A snow-white starling with black wingtips, a drooping crest and a patch of bare sky-blue skin around each eye, found wild only on Bali. Trapping for the cagebird trade pushed it to a handful of wild birds around 2000; releases have since rebuilt small populations.
nativeRange: Endemic to NW Bali, Indonesia (West Bali National Park); reintroduced to Nusa Penida and other Bali sites
abilities: Raises its long, lacy crest in display
Nests in tree holes, including old woodpecker and barbet holes
Survives in a strongly seasonal dry forest

animal.diet: Fruit, seeds, insects and other invertebrates
animal.habitat: Dry deciduous monsoon forest, acacia savanna and village edges
animal.behaviour: Pairs and small groups move through the canopy and forest edge, raising their crests and calling loudly.
fieldMarks: Almost entirely white starling
Black tips to the wings and tail
Bare bright blue skin around the eye
Long, drooping white crest; yellowish bill and blue-grey legs
animal.voice: Loud, varied chattering, harsh calls and whistles typical of starlings
animal.lookalikes: Black-winged myna (Java, Bali) has extensive black wings and a black tail and a yellow face patch; Javan white-eyes are tiny and green.
animal.whereToSee: West Bali National Park (Bali Barat), Nusa Penida island

lore: It is the official faunal symbol of Bali province. On Nusa Penida, Balinese villages agreed under traditional law (awig-awig) to protect released birds, a model for community-based conservation.
funFact: It was only described to science in 1912, and named after Walter Rothschild, the zoologist who owned the famous private museum at Tring.

otherNames: Lán hóu nǐ zhuómùniǎo 蓝喉拟啄木鸟 (Chinese)
summary: A bright green barbet with a sky-blue face and throat and a red crown crossed by a black band, whose loud rolling calls echo through Himalayan foothill forests. It is a fig specialist that carves its nest hole in dead wood.
nativeRange: Himalayan foothills from Uttarakhand through Nepal, Bhutan and NE India to Bangladesh, Myanmar, southern China, Thailand and Indochina
abilities: Disperses the seeds of figs and other fruiting trees
Excavates nest cavities in dead branches
Calls persistently from treetops through the breeding season

animal.diet: Figs and other fruit; some insects
animal.habitat: Broadleaf forest, forest edges, orchards and gardens, up to about 2,400 m
animal.behaviour: Sits motionless high in fruiting trees for long periods, so it is easier to hear than to see despite its colours.
fieldMarks: Stocky bright green barbet with a heavy bill, pale at the base with a dark upper mandible and tip
Sky-blue face, cheeks and throat
Red forehead and crown with a black band across the crown
Small red patch at the side of the throat
animal.voice: A loud, rolling 'took-a-rook, took-a-rook' or 'kutroo-kutroo', repeated endlessly
animal.lookalikes: Golden-throated barbet has a yellow throat; Great barbet is larger with a blue-black head and red vent; Coppersmith barbet is smaller with a yellow throat and red breast patch.
animal.whereToSee: Kathmandu valley gardens (Nepal), Corbett and Nainital (Uttarakhand), Darjeeling, Doi Inthanon (Thailand)
animal.season: Resident year-round; most vocal in spring

lore: Its incessant calling makes it one of the signature sounds of Himalayan hill stations such as Darjeeling and Kathmandu in spring.
funFact: Asian barbets were once placed in the same family as African and American barbets, but genetics showed they form a separate family, Megalaimidae.

otherNames: Hēi zhěn huánglí 黑枕黄鹂 (Chinese)
Kōraiuguisu コウライウグイス (Japanese)
summary: A brilliant golden-yellow bird with a black band running through the eye and around the nape, whose liquid fluting calls carry through gardens and woodland from China to Indonesia. Northern birds migrate south to winter in Southeast Asia and India.
nativeRange: Breeds from the Russian Far East, NE China and Korea south through eastern China; resident in Southeast Asia, the Philippines and Indonesia; winters in India (mainly south and northeast) and Southeast Asia
abilities: Weaves a hammock-like cup nest slung in a horizontal fork
Eats caterpillars, including hairy ones that many birds avoid
Long-distance migrant in the north of its range

animal.diet: Insects, caterpillars, fruit and berries, nectar
animal.habitat: Woodland, parks, gardens, plantations and mangroves
animal.behaviour: Stays high in the canopy and is often seen only as a flash of yellow in undulating flight between trees.
fieldMarks: Bright golden-yellow body
Broad black stripe through the eye that meets at the back of the head
Black wings with yellow edgings; black tail with yellow corners
Pinkish-red bill
animal.voice: Rich, liquid, fluty whistles such as 'lwee-wee-wee-leeow', and a harsh nasal 'kyaaa' alarm
animal.lookalikes: Indian golden oriole has a black mask only through the eye that does not join on the nape; Slender-billed oriole has a thinner bill and narrower nape band; females and young are greener with streaked underparts.
animal.whereToSee: Singapore and Kuala Lumpur parks year-round; Beijing and Seoul parks in summer; Andaman Islands year-round (resident race); scarce winter visitor to peninsular India
animal.season: Resident in Southeast Asia; summer visitor in northern China and Korea (May–Sep); winter visitor to India

lore: The huánglí in Du Fu's famous Tang-dynasty quatrain 'Two orioles sing in the green willows' (两个黄鹂鸣翠柳) is this species, and the bird has been a symbol of spring in Chinese poetry ever since.
funFact: Its Japanese name means 'Korean bush warbler', though it is not a warbler at all; in Japan it is only a scarce visitor.

summary: A sparrow-sized sandpiper with a unique spatula-shaped bill tip, breeding only on coastal tundra in Chukotka and northern Kamchatka and migrating around 8,000 km down the East Asian–Australasian Flyway to winter mainly in Bangladesh and Myanmar. Only around 400–450 adult birds survive.
nativeRange: Breeds in Chukotka and northern Kamchatka, Russia; migrates via the coasts of Japan, Korea and China (especially the Yellow Sea); winters mainly in Myanmar (Gulf of Mottama) and Bangladesh
abilities: Spoon-shaped bill tip used to sweep through soft mud for tiny invertebrates
Migrates about 8,000 km each way along the East Asian–Australasian Flyway
Depends on a few critical tidal mudflats as staging sites, especially in the Yellow Sea

animal.diet: Small invertebrates: worms, crustaceans, insect larvae; seeds on the breeding grounds
animal.habitat: Lagoon spits and coastal tundra when breeding; tidal mudflats on migration and in winter
animal.behaviour: Feeds with a sweeping side-to-side motion of the bill, like a tiny spoonbill, in shallow water and soft mud.
fieldMarks: Small, stint-sized sandpiper
Black bill broadening into a flat spatula at the tip (best seen head-on or in profile at close range)
Breeding: rufous head, neck and breast
Winter: pale grey above, white below, with a white forehead
animal.voice: A soft, rasping 'preep' in flight; males give a buzzing, trilling song in display flight on the breeding grounds
animal.lookalikes: Red-necked stint is almost identical in size and plumage but has a fine, pointed bill; check the bill tip carefully and watch for the sweeping feeding action.
animal.whereToSee: Gulf of Mottama (Martaban), Myanmar, and Sonadia Island, Bangladesh, in winter; Rudong and Tiaozini mudflats, Jiangsu, China, on migration
animal.season: Winter visitor to Bangladesh and Myanmar (Nov–Mar); passage migrant in China (Apr–May, Sep–Oct); breeds Jun–Aug in Chukotka

lore: Since 2012 a 'head-starting' project in Meinypilgyno, Chukotka, has collected eggs, hatched them in incubators and released fledglings to raise breeding success. The Tiaozini mudflats where it stages became part of China's Yellow Sea World Heritage site in 2019.
funFact: Its spoon-shaped bill is already present when the chick hatches.

otherNames: Rìběn shù yīng 日本树莺 (Chinese)
summary: A drab olive-brown warbler that hides in bamboo thickets but announces spring across Japan with its clear, rising whistle 'hoo-hokekyo'. It is so central to Japanese culture that its name became a byword for a beautiful voice.
nativeRange: Japan and nearby islands including Sakhalin and the Ryukyus; related forms in Korea, eastern China and Taiwan treated as part of this species by some authorities; introduced to Hawaii
abilities: Song carries far from deep cover despite the bird's small size
Males sing almost continuously through spring and summer
Introduced population thrives in Hawaiian forests

animal.diet: Insects and spiders; some nectar and fruit
animal.habitat: Dense undergrowth, bamboo thickets, scrub and forest edge from lowland to mountains
animal.size: About 14–16 cm long (males larger than females)
animal.behaviour: Skulks low in dense vegetation and is rarely seen in the open; in winter it moves to lower ground and gives only short 'chat' calls.
fieldMarks: Plain olive-brown upperparts and buffy-grey underparts
Pale eyebrow stripe
Rounded tail and short wings
Lacks the bright eye-ring and yellow-green tones of the Japanese white-eye
animal.voice: A long, rising whistle followed by an explosive flourish, written 'hoo-hokekyo'; also a rapid 'kekyo-kekyo-kekyo' sequence
animal.lookalikes: Japanese white-eye (mejiro) is brighter green with a white eye-ring and is often mistaken for the uguisu; Manchurian bush warbler is larger and browner.
animal.whereToSee: City parks and temple gardens throughout Japan in spring, e.g. Kyoto's Higashiyama and Tokyo's Meiji Jingu forest; also Oahu, Hawaii
animal.season: Resident; sings from late February to summer, in winter heard only as a call

lore: The Kokinshū (905) preface lists the uguisu singing among the blossoms as a voice of poetry, and its song is heard as 'Hokekyō', the Japanese name of the Lotus Sutra. Its droppings (uguisu no fun) were traditionally used in Japanese facial cosmetics.
funFact: The squeaking 'nightingale floors' (uguisubari) of Kyoto's Nijō Castle and Chion-in temple are named after the bird's chirping.

otherNames: Bái xiōng fěicuì 白胸翡翠 (Chinese)
summary: A big-billed kingfisher with a chocolate head, a brilliant turquoise back and a shining white bib, often seen far from water on wires above fields. It eats lizards, crabs, insects and even small snakes as readily as fish.
nativeRange: Turkey, the Levant and Iraq through Iran, Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh to southern China, Southeast Asia and the Philippines
abilities: Hunts on dry land as well as in water, taking lizards, frogs, mice and large insects
Digs a nest tunnel in earth banks with its bill
Beats large prey against a perch before swallowing

animal.diet: Large insects, lizards, frogs, crabs, fish, small snakes, rodents and occasionally small birds
animal.habitat: Open country, canals, rice fields, gardens, mangroves and forest edge
animal.behaviour: Perches conspicuously on wires and posts, dropping to the ground for prey; displays from treetops with wings spread to show the white patches.
fieldMarks: Large kingfisher with a massive red bill
Chocolate-brown head and belly, sharply defined white throat and breast
Brilliant turquoise-blue back, wings and tail
Large white wing patches visible in flight
animal.voice: A loud, shrill, whinnying 'kililili' trill, given from perches and in flight
animal.lookalikes: Stork-billed kingfisher is larger with an ochre head and body; Black-capped kingfisher has a black cap and white collar; Common kingfisher is tiny with orange underparts.
animal.whereToSee: Canals and fields across Punjab and Sindh, Keoladeo, Sri Lankan paddies; Lahore and Delhi gardens

lore: It is the state bird of West Bengal. The species name smyrnensis refers to Smyrna (modern Izmir) in Turkey, from where the first specimen described came.
funFact: Despite being a kingfisher, it often lives far from any water, hunting lizards and insects in dry fields.

summary: A massive hornbill with a solid, ivory-like casque on its forehead and two very long central tail feathers, whose accelerating hooting call ends in a burst of maniacal laughter. Hunted for 'red ivory', it was uplisted straight from Near Threatened to Critically Endangered in 2015.
nativeRange: Southern Myanmar and Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra and Borneo
abilities: The only hornbill with a solid casque, used in head-butting aerial contests between males
Call is one of the loudest in Asian rainforests
Disperses the seeds of strangler figs

animal.diet: Mainly figs; also small animals
animal.habitat: Tall lowland and hill dipterocarp rainforest
animal.size: About 110–120 cm long, plus central tail feathers up to about 50 cm
animal.behaviour: Males clash in flight, striking their casques together with a loud crack; the female seals herself into a tree hole to nest.
fieldMarks: Very large brown-black hornbill with white belly and white tail with a black band
Short, deep red casque and yellow-and-red bill; casque is solid
Bare wrinkled throat skin, red in males and pale bluish in females
Two very long, white central tail feathers trailing behind
animal.voice: A long series of loud 'took' notes, spaced at first and accelerating, ending in a cackling, laugh-like crescendo
animal.lookalikes: Rhinoceros hornbill has a large upturned orange casque and no long tail plumes; Great hornbill has a flat yellow casque and a white neck.
animal.whereToSee: Danum Valley and Tabin (Sabah), Gunung Leuser (Sumatra), Budo-Sungai Padi (Thailand)

lore: Its solid casque, 'hornbill ivory' (ho-ting in Chinese), was carved into belt buckles, snuff bottles and ornaments during the Ming and Qing dynasties and traded from Borneo for centuries. In Borneo, the Iban and other Dayak peoples revered the bird and wore its tail feathers.
funFact: Its Malay name 'tebang mentua' comes from a folk tale of a man who chopped down the posts of his mother-in-law's house while she was inside and was turned into the bird: the call's accelerating 'took' notes are his axe blows, and the final cackle is his laughter as the house falls.

otherNames: Hóng fù jǐnjī 红腹锦鸡 (Chinese)
summary: One of the most brilliantly coloured birds in the world: the male has a golden crest, a scarlet body, a cape of orange feathers barred with black and a very long, mottled tail. Despite its colours it is a shy bird of dense mountain thickets in central China.
nativeRange: Mountains of central and western China (Gansu, Shaanxi, Sichuan, Hubei, Guizhou and neighbouring provinces); feral populations in Britain
abilities: Male spreads his golden-and-black cape into a fan around the face during courtship
Lives in dense bamboo and scrub where its colours are surprisingly hard to see
Roosts in trees at night

animal.diet: Seeds, leaves, shoots, berries and invertebrates
animal.habitat: Dense young forest, bamboo and scrub on mountainsides
animal.size: Males about 90–105 cm including the long tail; females 60–80 cm
animal.behaviour: Very secretive in the wild; males display to females by fanning the cape sideways and showing it from different angles.
fieldMarks: Male: golden-yellow crest and rump, scarlet underparts
Male: orange cape barred with black, green upper back
Very long, cinnamon tail with dark spots
Female: barred buff-brown with a long tail
animal.voice: A harsh, metallic 'cha-chak' call in spring
animal.lookalikes: Lady Amherst's pheasant male is white, black and green with a white cape barred black; hybrids between the two are common in captivity.
animal.whereToSee: Foping and Changqing reserves in the Qinling Mountains, Shaanxi; Wolong in Sichuan

lore: In Ming and Qing China, the golden pheasant was embroidered on the 'mandarin square' badges of second-rank civil officials. It is widely kept in aviaries and has been in European collections since at least the 18th century.
funFact: Linnaeus described it in 1758 in the first edition of Systema Naturae where modern zoological names begin.

summary: A tern-like bird with a bright orange bill whose lower half is longer than the upper, which it slices through the water surface in flight to snap up fish. It nests on sandbars of big South Asian rivers that are increasingly disturbed by people and dams.
nativeRange: Rivers of India and Bangladesh (notably the Chambal and Ganges systems), with wintering on the Bangladesh coast; formerly the Indus in Pakistan and the Irrawaddy and Mekong
abilities: Skims with its long lower mandible cutting the water, snapping shut on contact with fish
Its pupils are vertical slits, unusual among birds, which may reduce glare from water
Feeds at dusk and at night as well as by day

animal.diet: Small fish and crustaceans
animal.habitat: Large rivers with sandbars; estuaries and coasts in winter
animal.behaviour: Flies low over calm water with the lower bill slicing the surface; nests in colonies in scrapes on exposed sandbars in spring.
fieldMarks: Black cap and upperparts with a white forehead, collar and underparts
Deep orange-red bill with a yellow tip, lower mandible much longer than upper
Long, pointed wings with a white trailing edge
Short, red legs
animal.voice: Nasal, yapping 'kap-kap' calls, especially at colonies
animal.lookalikes: River tern has a yellow, evenly-sized bill and a grey back; Black-bellied tern is smaller with a black belly in breeding plumage.
animal.whereToSee: National Chambal Sanctuary (Madhya Pradesh/Rajasthan/Uttar Pradesh); Padma and Meghna rivers and the Bangladesh coast in winter
animal.season: Resident with local movements; breeds March–May on river sandbars

lore: It was once recorded on the Indus in Pakistan and on Myanmar's rivers, but damming, sand-mining and disturbance of river islands have left it rare or absent there.
funFact: Skimmers are the only birds with a lower mandible longer than the upper.

summary: A vivid magpie of Sri Lanka's wet-zone rainforests with an ultramarine body, chestnut head and wings, and a long white-tipped tail. It lives in family groups that raise young cooperatively.
nativeRange: Endemic to the wet zone and central hills of Sri Lanka
abilities: Breeds cooperatively, with helpers assisting the breeding pair
Joins mixed-species foraging flocks in the rainforest
Hunts large insects, frogs and lizards in the canopy

animal.diet: Insects, frogs, small lizards and fruit
animal.habitat: Undisturbed wet evergreen forest, from lowlands to about 2,100 m
animal.size: About 42–47 cm long including the tail
animal.behaviour: Groups move noisily through the mid-canopy; at Sinharaja they can be approached quite closely along forest trails.
fieldMarks: Bright cobalt-blue body and long blue tail with white tips
Rich chestnut head, wings and neck
Bright red bill, legs and eye-ring
Long, graduated tail
animal.voice: Loud, varied calls including a ringing 'chink-chink' and harsh, rasping notes
animal.lookalikes: No similar bird in Sri Lanka; Red-billed blue magpie of the Himalaya has a black head and does not occur on the island.
animal.whereToSee: Sinharaja Forest Reserve, Horton Plains and Kitulgala, Sri Lanka

lore: It is one of Sri Lanka's most sought-after endemic birds for visiting birdwatchers, and Sinharaja's mixed feeding flocks, often led by its calls, are a classic of tropical ornithology.
funFact: Surveys in 2004–2006 estimated only about 10,000–20,000 individuals left.

summary: A rare bustard of tall floodplain grasslands, whose black male leaps above the grass in spectacular display flights showing almost wholly white wings. Fewer than about 1,000 survive in two populations, in the Indian subcontinent and in Cambodia.
nativeRange: Terai and Brahmaputra floodplain grasslands of Nepal and NE India (Assam, Uttar Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh); a separate subspecies in Cambodia and southern Vietnam
abilities: Males spring high above the grass in display, gliding back down with a whirr of wings
Females raise chicks alone, hidden in tall grass
Depends on grassland maintained by floods and fire

animal.diet: Grasshoppers, beetles, ants and other insects; shoots, seeds and flowers
animal.habitat: Tall, wet alluvial grassland interspersed with shorter grass
animal.behaviour: Males hold display territories in short grass patches in spring, leaping vertically into the air repeatedly at dawn and dusk.
fieldMarks: Male: black head, neck and underparts with a slight crest
Male: wings almost entirely white, conspicuous in flight
Female: buff-brown and heavily patterned, larger than the male
Long legs and neck; walks upright through grass
animal.voice: Usually silent; a metallic 'chik-chik' when flushed
animal.lookalikes: Lesser florican (India) is smaller and males have long head plumes and a white collar; female Lesser florican is smaller and more slender.
animal.whereToSee: Kaziranga and Manas (Assam), Dudhwa (Uttar Pradesh), Shuklaphanta and Koshi Tappu (Nepal), Tonle Sap grasslands (Cambodia)
animal.season: Resident; best seen during displays Mar–May

lore: Colonial-era hunters prized it as a gamebird, and the drainage and ploughing of floodplain grasslands since have reduced it to protected reserves.
funFact: Unlike most bustards, the female is larger than the male.

summary: A grey shorebird with a crimson, down-curved bill and a black face and breast band, living on the shingle beds of fast mountain rivers across High Asia. It is so distinct that it sits in a family of its own.
nativeRange: Mountains of Central and High Asia: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan through northern Pakistan, Ladakh, Nepal, Bhutan and Tibet to northern and central China
abilities: Probes under stones in fast-flowing glacial rivers for larvae
Camouflaged grey plumage matches river shingle
Breeds at altitudes up to about 4,400 m

animal.diet: Aquatic insects and larvae, small fish and crustaceans
animal.habitat: Shingle and stony braided river beds in mountain valleys, roughly 1,700–4,400 m
animal.behaviour: Wades in rushing water, reaching under stones with its curved bill; very hard to spot until it moves.
fieldMarks: Grey-brown upperparts and grey neck and breast
Long, down-curved crimson bill
Black face and black breast band bordered with white
Red legs (duller outside breeding season)
animal.voice: A ringing, whistled 'klee-klee' and a 'tee-tee-tee' trill, carrying over the noise of rivers
animal.lookalikes: No real lookalike: curlews and whimbrels are brown, streaked and lack the black breast band and red bill.
animal.whereToSee: Hunza and Chitral rivers in northern Pakistan; Indus valley near Leh in Ladakh; Langtang and Mustang in Nepal; mountain rivers near Beijing in winter
animal.season: Resident, moving to lower river valleys in winter

lore: It is a prize sighting for birders visiting the Karakoram and Ladakh, where its grey plumage vanishes against river stones.
funFact: It is the only member of the family Ibidorhynchidae.

otherNames: Hóng zuǐ lán què 红嘴蓝鹊 (Chinese)
summary: A long-tailed magpie of Himalayan and Chinese hill forests with a black hood, white nape, lavender-blue back and a tail longer than its body, tipped in white. Bold and noisy, it raids nests and visits campsites for scraps.
nativeRange: Western Himalaya (Himachal Pradesh) east through Nepal, Bhutan and NE India to Myanmar, much of eastern China and Indochina
abilities: Raids nests of other birds for eggs and nestlings
Caches food in the ground or crevices
Groups mob predators loudly

animal.diet: Insects, fruit, eggs and nestlings, small reptiles, carrion and scraps
animal.habitat: Broadleaf and mixed hill forest, forest edge, villages and parks
animal.size: About 65–68 cm long including a tail of around 45 cm
animal.behaviour: Small groups follow one another in a straggling line between trees, long tails streaming behind.
fieldMarks: Black head and breast with a white patch on the crown and nape
Lavender-blue back and wings
Very long, graduated blue tail with white tips and black bands
Bright red bill and legs
animal.voice: Loud, varied calls including a harsh 'chuk-chuk' and a ringing 'pit-pit-pitpit'
animal.lookalikes: Yellow-billed blue magpie (western Himalaya, higher altitudes) has a yellow bill and smaller white nape patch; Common green magpie is green with a red bill.
animal.whereToSee: Kathmandu valley forests (Shivapuri), Corbett and Nainital (India), Beijing's Fragrant Hills

lore: It is a common park bird in central and southern China and a familiar subject in Chinese bird-and-flower painting.
funFact: Its tail can be roughly two-thirds of its total length.

otherNames: Zōng bèi bóláo 棕背伯劳 (Chinese)
summary: A predatory songbird with a black bandit mask and a rufous back, which perches on bushes and wires to pounce on insects, lizards and small birds. Like other shrikes it impales surplus prey on thorns as a larder.
nativeRange: Kazakhstan and Iran through Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka and Nepal to China, Southeast Asia and New Guinea
abilities: Impales prey on thorns and barbed wire for storage and to tear it apart
Mimics the calls of other birds within its song
Takes vertebrate prey as large as small birds and mice

animal.diet: Large insects, lizards, small birds, rodents and frogs
animal.habitat: Open scrub, cultivation, gardens and hedgerows
animal.behaviour: Sits upright on exposed perches, swinging its long tail, then drops on prey; males defend territories with harsh calls and songs full of mimicry.
fieldMarks: Black mask through the eye, grey crown and nape
Rufous back, rump and flanks
Long, graduated black tail with pale edges
Hooked black bill; small white wing patch
animal.voice: Harsh 'chaak' and grating calls; song is a quiet, rambling warble with much mimicry
animal.lookalikes: Bay-backed shrike is smaller with a black forehead and maroon back; Isabelline shrike is sandy-brown; Grey-backed shrike (Himalaya) has an all-grey back.
animal.whereToSee: Hedgerows and farmland across Punjab, Islamabad's sector parks and northern Pakistan valleys in summer; widespread in India and Sri Lanka in winter
animal.season: Resident or partly migratory; northern breeders move south in winter

lore: The shrike habit of impaling prey earned the family the English folk name 'butcher-bird'.

summary: Sri Lanka's national bird, a wild relative of the chicken whose rooster glows orange-red and gold with a red comb marked by a yellow centre. It is endemic to the island and common in its national parks.
nativeRange: Endemic to Sri Lanka
abilities: Hybridises occasionally with domestic chickens
Lives in both the wet and dry zones of Sri Lanka, from sea level to the hills
Forages by scratching leaf litter for seeds and insects

animal.diet: Seeds, grain, berries, insects and other invertebrates
animal.habitat: Forest, scrub jungle and plantations
animal.size: Males about 66–73 cm; females about 35 cm
animal.behaviour: Roosters crow at dawn and dusk from perches; birds often feed in the open along park roads in the early morning.
fieldMarks: Male: orange-red body with golden neck hackles
Male: red comb with a central yellow patch; red wattles
Male: dark purple-black wings and arching tail
Female: mottled brown with patterned wings
animal.voice: A distinctive crow 'chuck-chraw-choyik', quite unlike the domestic cockerel's crow
animal.lookalikes: Red junglefowl and domestic chickens have an all-red comb and a different crow; feral chickens near villages can cause confusion.
animal.whereToSee: Sinharaja, Yala, Udawalawe and Horton Plains national parks

lore: It is the national bird of Sri Lanka and appears on Sri Lankan postage stamps.
funFact: It is one of four wild Gallus species; the domestic chicken descends mainly from the Red junglefowl, but genes from the Grey and Sri Lanka junglefowl have been found in some domestic breeds.
